title: The Character I Almost Overlooked: The Woman of Tekoa
paragraphs: The Character I Almost Overlooked: The Woman of Tekoa
She walked into David’s story wearing wisdom like a blade wrapped in velvet.
And most people scroll right past her.

The Woman of Tekoa is not a famous queen.
Not a prophet with a book.
Not a miracle-worker.
Just a nameless woman sent to speak when a kingdom was breaking from the inside.
That is exactly why she matters.

In 2 Samuel 14, Joab recruits her to approach King David with a story—a grieving widow, two sons, one dead, one condemned. At first it feels like strategy. Almost political theater. But then the trap closes. The story is not just about her “case.” It is about David’s own house. His estranged son Absalom. His unresolved grief. His half-buried guilt. His paralyzed leadership.

And this woman?
She sees it.

She speaks with courage in a room where power could crush her.
She uses story to slip past a king’s defenses.
She names the ache no one else is naming.
That’s dangerous holy work.
But here’s what we miss:

The Woman of Tekoa is easy to admire for her eloquence and overlook for what she exposes in us.
Because David is not the only one who delays obedience.
Not the only one who knows what is broken and still keeps postponing the hard, righteous thing.
Not the only one who lets pain sit too long until it grows teeth.
We do it too.

We excuse it.
Spiritualize it.
Rename it “waiting on God” when sometimes it is just fear wearing church clothes.

The woman from Tekoa reminds us that God can use unexpected voices to confront hidden fractures.
A nameless woman.
A wise mouth.
A piercing story.
And a king who could not hide forever.

Still, this passage is not ultimately about her brilliance.
And it is not about David’s failure alone.

It points us to the deeper ache of the human heart:
we need more than clever words.
We need more than delayed reconciliation.
We need more than partial justice.
We need a better King.

David brought Absalom back to Jerusalem, but did not fully restore what was broken. The reunion was incomplete. Tense. Fragile. And later, the damage erupted. Why? Because human wisdom, even when sharp, cannot heal sin at the root.
Only Jesus can do that.

Where David hesitated, Jesus moves toward rebels.
Where David’s house fractured, Jesus builds a family by grace.
Where earthly kings manage appearances, Christ carries our guilt to the cross.
He does not merely bring us near geographically.
He brings us near to God through His blood.
That is the Gospel.

You may feel overlooked.
Unnamed.
Sent into spaces where nobody expects much from you.
Do not despise that place.
God has always loved using unlikely voices to awaken sleeping hearts.

And maybe this is the deeper scandal:
the character you almost overlooked may be the one God uses to expose the truth you almost refused to face.

So read her again.
Slowly.

Then ask:
What truth have I delayed?
What fracture have I baptized with excuses?
What mercy is Christ calling me to finally receive—and extend?

There is hope here.
Even for the silent house.
Even for the compromised leader.
Even for the heart full of unfinished business.

Jesus does not deal in halfway restoration.
He makes dead things live again.

“God devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast” (2 Samuel 14:14).
That longing whispers forward to Christ.
